title: Entanglement-of-formation potentials for feedback-assisted classical communication and randomness distillation
abstract: We develop entanglement-of-formation potentials for feedback-assisted classical communication and one-way randomness distillation. For a finite-dimensional quantum channel without initial shared entanglement, an exact amortization theorem bounds the increase of message information plus entanglement remaining across the communicating laboratories. This proves a classical-feedback capacity bound using a mixed-convex-roof expression previously studied by Winter and Yang in the context of potential capacities. We determine the capacity of flagged mixtures of noiseless and entanglement-breaking channels, improve a published depolarizing-channel converse, and evaluate the new bound exactly for the amplitude damping channel. A state analogue gives a finite-blocklength upper bound on the net shared randomness obtainable with one-way classical communication. Amplitude-damping Choi states provide exact benchmarks, while a full-rank generalized amplitude-damping Choi state demonstrates a useful improvement where we do not evaluate the operational rate exactly. We also distinguish one-way from two-way randomness distillation: a two-round weak-measurement protocol strictly exceeds the exact one-way rate of every nontrivial qubit isotropic state. The protocol preserves quantum side information during its first decoding and extracts additional randomness in the reverse direction. This shows why the one-way state potential is not a general two-way converse. Together, these results establish a common entanglement-based approach to sharper communication and randomness bounds, while revealing how retained quantum correlations enable two-way distillation to surpass one-way limits.
summary: This work introduces entanglement-of-formation potentials to derive sharper, entanglement-based upper bounds for classical communication rates and randomness distillation. The authors prove key capacity theorems for specific quantum channels and crucially distinguish between one-way and two-way randomness extraction, showing the latter can exceed the former's limits.
main_problem: The paper develops entanglement-of-formation potentials to establish tighter theoretical bounds for classical communication assisted by feedback and for one-way randomness distillation.
main_result: It establishes an exact amortization theorem for the classical-feedback capacity and demonstrates that two-way randomness distillation protocols can surpass the limits set by one-way state potentials.
method: The authors employ potential-based methods, utilizing mixed-convex-roof expressions and rigorous information-theoretic accounting to bound achievable rates.
model_or_system: The analysis focuses on general quantum channels, specifically examining the amplitude damping and depolarizing channels, and considering communication protocols involving feedback and state distillation.
key_observables: Message information, remaining entanglement, classical-feedback capacity, net shared randomness, and the entanglement-of-formation potential ($U_F$ or $V_F$).
important_parameters: The fidelity of the bound depends on the specific quantum channel parameters (e.g., damping coefficients $\gamma$ or depolarizing parameters $p$).
main_assumptions: The primary limitation noted is that the one-way state potential is not a general converse for two-way distillation, which is shown by a specific two-round protocol.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the adaptive structure of classical communication with receiver-to-sender feedback, showing the flow of quantum and classical information.
paper_structure: The paper builds from developing the potential framework for feedback capacity (using mixed-convex-roof expressions) to applying this framework to specific channels, and finally contrasting one-way versus two-way randomness distillation protocols.
why_interesting: The rigorous bounding techniques developed here—especially the use of entanglement potentials—provide powerful, general tools for quantifying resource limitations in quantum communication, which is fundamental to quantum information theory.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Classical communication with receiver-to-sender feedback. Alice’s later input depends on Bob’s earlier classical outcome. Each party may retain quantum memory, and earlier forward transmissions may entangle those memories. Time flows from left to right. Forward quantum systems move diagonally down and right, while the classical feedback moves up and right. Solid arrows indicate quantum systems and dashed arrows classical communication. No initial shared entanglement or free forward classical communication is supplied. Figure 4 later adds the state and potential labels used in the converse.

Figure 2: The two contributions to the potential in a two-use noiseless example. Initially both Bell shares are at Alice. The first forward qubit leaves a shared Bell state but no message information at Bob. After Pauli encoding and the second forward qubit, all four Bell states are at Bob and can be distinguished perfectly. The entanglement remaining across the laboratories has been consumed. The forward transfers move diagonally down and right; the horizontal wire retains a Bell share locally.

Figure 3: Two bipartitions of σA′B′B. The physical output cut is A′|B′B. In the comparison cut A′B′|B, both old memories are treated mathematically as the reference for the transmitted input. The correction in Lemma 4.1 is S(B′|B), which may be negative. The comparison does not grant free transmission of Bob’s old memory.

Figure 4: Three uses of N : Ai →Bi with classical feedback. Retained memories carry primes. The pre-channel state ρ(i) contains A′ iAi at Alice and B′ i at Bob; the post-channel state ω(i) contains A′ i at Alice and B′ iBi at Bob. The dotted markers label these complete states, not only the adjacent wire. Each interval between uses contains the receiver instrument, classical feedback, and the next encoder. The converse bounds Q+ i −Q− i at every channel use and Q− i+1 −Q+ i between uses. The initial seed is suppressed.

Figure 5: The potential increases only at forward channel uses. One representative forward use and the subsequent local-processing interval are shown. The notation Q− i and Q+ i denotes the pre- and post-channel values marked in the detailed protocol of Figure 4. Each forward increment is at most UF(N); each intervening local/feedback increment is nonpositive. Adding all increments gives the explicit telescoping estimate in the proof of Theorem 4.3.
